sub: Ship design compliance checking · Meyer Turku challenge · Since AI Hackathon 2026
say: This video walks through RuleTrace and the RuleMate Copilot, built for the Meyer Turku challenge at the Since AI Hackathon.
The goal is to check ship designs against the regulations, show exactly why something fails, and keep engineers in control of every decision.
RuleTrace opens with three steps: load a ship design, see the problems on the model, and click a problem to see the rule, what was required, and how to fix it.
A design can come from a general arrangement drawing, an IFC 3D model, or a structured design file.
On the left are the designs already checked, and at the top you choose who is signed in.
Here is the demo cruise ship. Every part is drawn in 3D and coloured by its result: red fails, orange is a warning, grey cannot be checked yet, and green passes.
On the right are the findings: eleven fails, two warnings, one that cannot be checked, and sixteen passes.
Nothing is accepted automatically. Every open finding needs an engineer's review.
Clicking a finding zooms to the part. This accessible cabin door has a twenty-five millimetre threshold, and the ADA standards allow at most twelve point seven.
The panel shows what was required, what the design has, why it matters, how to fix it, and the exact rule text, checked against the published source.
Every comparison is done in code, not by an AI model.
The engineer then decides. Confirming that it must be fixed records the decision with the person's name and the time, in a tamper-evident audit chain.
Sign-off needs every finding reviewed, and the approval of a second person.
The ship profile decides which rules apply: ship type, passengers, size, gross tonnage, flag and keel-laying date.
Tick where the ship will operate, for example US ports or emission control areas, and check again. Rules such as the ADA accessibility standards switch on or off.
Compare two revisions shows what a new design revision fixed, and whether it broke anything.
Here twelve problems are fixed, two are still open, and one check got worse: a main vertical zone is now forty-five metres, over the forty metre limit.
Knock-on effects like this are easy to miss by hand.
RuleTrace also reads general arrangement drawings. From this PDF it measured the scale, found the rooms and the deck heights, and built the 3D design.
It even compares the plan with the drawing's own title block: the plan shows two double cabins, but the text says three.
The dashboard summarises every checked design: problems to fix, checks that need more data, and the status of human approval.
Nothing counts as approved until a second person has signed it off.
Signed in as Aino, the compliance lead, the same data becomes a compliance posture.
It shows open issues by severity, how many rules are verified against the official text, how much could be checked, and whether the saved history is intact.
The administrator sees who can do what, the health of the system, and anything that needs attention.
New rule sets lets you test a company, owner or class requirement document before using it.
RuleTrace turns each measurable shall into a draft check, runs it on the designs, and compares it with today's rules.
This sample owner's standard has four flawed rules, for example a corridor width weaker than the current requirement. Nothing is added to the live rules without people.

sub: Ask the regulations · check values · browse clauses · confidential by default
say: Next, the RuleMate Copilot, the assistant inside RuleTrace.
The Copilot opens beside the 3D view. It is in confidential mode by default: nothing leaves this computer.
Answers come from a local model running in Ollama. Cloud models and Google Gemini are switched off, even if keys are set.
It searches the full regulation texts: the ADA and ABA requirements, 46 CFR Part 190 for research vessels, and the Maritime Labour Convention, about two thousand clauses.
Ask a question in plain language. Every sentence of the answer must cite a clause that supports it, and every number, unit and quote must be in that clause. This is checked in code.
If a draft fails the checks, the clause text is shown instead.
Values the model left out are added below, quoted word for word from the cited clauses, so no number goes missing.
This answer comes from the Maritime Labour Convention: at least two hundred and three centimetres of headroom, Standard A 3.1, paragraph 6 a.
Click a citation to read the clause itself.
Questions outside the loaded rules still get an answer, clearly labelled as general knowledge and not verified.
The model must name its sources, and code checks each one: a clause of a loaded text, a known instrument such as SOLAS that is not loaded, or a source that cannot be identified.
An engineer approves or rejects the answer, and the decision is written to the audit log.
Check values compares design values with the limits in the full texts. Upload a CSV file, a picture or a drawing page, or type the values in.
The summary says in plain words what breaks a rule, and what to do next.
This chart compares each design value with its limit, in the same unit. The bar is the design, the black line is the limit.
A fifteen hundred millimetre turning circle is fifty-nine point zero six inches, just under the sixty inch minimum, so it fails.
Pass and fail are always computed in code. Items with a condition go to an engineer for approval.
Browse shows the full texts as an outline with search. Each clause shows its context, its parent, its sub-clauses and its references.
Here, the minimum floor area of a single-berth cabin, which depends on the size of the ship.
Gemini is optional and kept separate from the bot. It reads drawings and pictures, and code confirms every reading on the image.
In confidential mode it is off, so drawings never leave the computer.
For public documents only, an engineer can switch confidential mode off for sixty minutes, after confirming that no Meyer data is used and giving a reason.
It switches back on by itself, every switch is in the audit log, and an installation can lock it on.
ACCURACY

sub: Checked in code · traceable to a clause · approved by people · confidential by default
say: To sum up. RuleTrace checks designs and shows on the model why something fails.
The Copilot answers from the full regulation texts, with every citation and number checked in code.
Engineers approve every decision, and in confidential mode everything stays on this computer.
